analysis.one_liner: Restores a 35% top corporate tax rate and closes loopholes that let multinationals shift profits offshore.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past its committee referral; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would undo major pieces of the 2017 corporate tax law. It would restore the old graduated corporate rates topping out at 35% (the rate is now a flat 21%), and tax the foreign profits of US-owned overseas subsidiaries immediately instead of letting companies leave them offshore untaxed until brought home. It would also limit interest deductions that multinationals use to shrink their US tax bill, tighten rules on companies that reincorporate abroad while staying run from the US, cut tax credits that oil, gas, and mining companies claim for payments to foreign governments, and repeal a deduction for income from foreign-held intangible assets like patents.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gain would flow to the US Treasury through higher taxes on large multinational corporations, which fund government services. Domestic-only companies would also benefit from a more level playing field, since they cannot shift profits to low-tax countries the way multinationals can.

how_it_helps.text: Restores graduated corporate tax rates of 15% to 35%, replacing the flat 21% rate set in 2017, with the top rate applying to income above $10 million [S2].

Treats all income of controlled foreign corporations (foreign subsidiaries of US companies) as taxable subpart F income, ending the deferral that lets companies leave foreign profits untaxed by the US until repatriated [S2].
Limits interest deductions for members of large international corporate groups, a rule aimed at earnings-stripping, where US subsidiaries load up on intra-group debt to erase taxable income [S2].

Treats foreign corporations that are managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, and tightens the anti-inversion rules for companies that move their legal domicile abroad [S2].

Repeals the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income and limits foreign tax credits for 'dual capacity' taxpayers in oil, gas, and mining who pay levies to foreign governments in exchange for specific economic benefits [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational corporations and their shareholders would bear the cost through higher US tax bills, particularly companies that currently shift profits to low-tax foreign jurisdictions or hold earnings in overseas subsidiaries.

drawbacks.text: Raising the top corporate rate back to 35% would increase the tax burden on US-headquartered multinationals, and opponents argue this could reduce domestic investment or push more corporate activity and headquarters offshore [S2].

Taxing all foreign subsidiary income immediately would eliminate deferral entirely, a bigger departure than current law that could put US-based companies at a competitive disadvantage against foreign rivals not subject to it [S2].

The bill would override US treaty obligations to deny certain treaty benefits and limit dual-capacity foreign tax credits, which could expose US companies to double taxation abroad and invite retaliation from trading partners [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would substantially raise revenue from large multinationals and close well-documented profit-shifting channels, but it goes further than most mainstream proposals — full deferral repeal, a 35% top rate, and treaty overrides carry real risks of double taxation, competitive disadvantage, and international friction. Its design reflects a maximal position, which likely contributed to its lack of cosponsors.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Sanders introduced the bill and it was sent to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on April 10, 2024 and read twice before being referred to the Committee on Finance [S1][S4].
No further action was ever taken: the Finance Committee held no markup, reported no vote, and the Senate never considered it [S4].
No other senator signed on as a cosponsor — the bill ended with zero [S3].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died without ever receiving a committee or floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large multinational corporations that would have faced higher US taxes under the bill are better off, since the proposal died without any of its provisions taking effect. The 21% flat corporate rate and existing offshore profit-shifting rules remain unchanged.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Multinational corporations dodging the tax changes

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Corporate Tax Dodging Prevention Act in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on April 10, 2024 and took no further action — no markup, no vote, no report — before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split is visible in the record; the bill drew a single independent sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party [S3].

industries.note: The bill's core purpose is to end tax advantages these companies get from shifting profits to low-tax countries, deferring tax on foreign earnings, and deducting intra-group interest. Their savings under current law come at the expense of US tax revenue.

industries.industry: Oil, gas, and mining companies operating abroad
industries.note: The bill would limit the foreign tax credits 'dual capacity' taxpayers claim for payments to foreign governments that come bundled with specific economic benefits, such as resource extraction rights.

industries.industry: Companies reincorporating abroad while run from the US
industries.note: Tighter anti-inversion rules and a new managed-and-controlled test would tax such companies as domestic, closing a route used to escape US tax on worldwide income.
